source.title_on_document: Facilitating Asynchronous Idea Generation and Selection with Chatbots

supplement.where: Appendices A-D, PDF pp. 25-29. Section 5 (p. 9) refers to technical descriptions and evaluations in Appendices A and B. Appendix C (p. 27) also refers to Supplementary.C without a separate usable link.
supplement.holds: Classifier implementation, prediction and latency benchmarks (Appendix A.1-A.2, p. 25), human calibration of similarity thresholds (A.3, p. 26), bandit algorithm, actions and rewards (B-D, pp. 26-28), and simulated evaluations (D.1, pp. 28-29). These appendices do not report participant-level standard errors for the main experimental contrasts; the standard-error formula in Appendix D defines a bandit reward from idea ratings.

paper_design_summary: Study 1 randomly assigned 48 people, 24 per group, to structured or adaptive Telegram chatbot facilitators for five days of asynchronous pandemic-related ideation, measuring idea counts, similarity to a fixed seed idea, self-ratings and surveys (pp. 11-15, Sections 6-7). Study 2 interviewed an expert after an hour-long human-facilitated workshop, reported as 11 participants despite demographic counts of 8 men and 4 women, and compared its notable-idea proportions and seed similarity with the reused Study 1 groups without reported random assignment to the human baseline (pp. 17-18, Section 8 and Fig. 11). The deployed chatbots retrieved other collaborators' ideas using a fine-tuned DistilBERT classifier and, for adaptive facilitation, a bandit algorithm; GPT-4 was tested only in classifier benchmarks, with separate human threshold calibration and simulated bandit evaluations in the appendices (p. 9, Section 5.1; pp. 25-29, Appendices A-D).

studies.label: User study: structured vs adaptive chatbot facilitator (asynchronous ideation)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Which chatbot facilitator a participant interacted with: structured or adaptive
assignment.quote: We randomly assigned half of them to interact with either the structured or adaptive facilitator, considering gender balance.

arms.name: Structured facilitator
arms.description: Chatbot gives every user the same process: first shows dissimilar ideas and asks for any new idea, then shows similar ideas and asks to improve one; in selection, presents ideas in descending order of ratings.

arms.name: Adaptive facilitator
arms.description: Chatbot uses a multi-armed bandit to choose inspirations and ideation methods based on the user's ideation performance, and to order ideas during selection.

participants.who: Adults recruited via social network who had experienced collaborative ideation (mean age 27.21); backgrounds included teachers, software developers, researchers, and nurses. No exclusions are reported; the satisfaction results refer to 'out of 24 participants' per group (p. 15).
participants.quote: We recruited 48 participants via social network (Mean age = 27.21, SD = 4.95, self-identified as men = 21 and women = 27), who had experienced any type of collaborative ideation
participants.locator: p. 11, Section 6.2 Participants; Fig. 6 (Structured facilitator group (N = 24), Adaptive facilitator group (N = 24))

ai_tool.name_model: Custom Telegram chatbots written in Python; fine-tuned DistilBERT semantic-similarity classifier (GPT-4 tested but not used); adaptive bot adds a multi-armed bandit

task.description: Asynchronous group ideation over five days: two days of idea generation, two days of idea selection, then review of the three top-rated ideas; goal was ideas to improve daily life during a pandemic.

outcomes.name: Semantic similarity of each idea to one seed idea ('A clear mask that allows people to see your expressions'), scored 0-5 by the fine-tuned DistilBERT classifier; higher = more similar
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: A learned semantic-textual-similarity prediction from DistilBERT base-uncased, fine-tuned on the English portion of SemEval2017-STS using mean-squared-error loss (p. 25, Appendix A). Each generated idea is scored against the single seed, A clear mask that allows people to see your expressions (p. 13, Section 7.2.1). Section 5.1 (p. 9) calls this a 5-point scale; Fig. 9 (p. 14) displays similarity scores from 0 to 5. The paper does not specify an embedding-distance or cosine-similarity calculation for this outcome. This is similarity to a fixed seed, not diversity across different participants' outputs.

contrasts.reported: Mean idea similarity: structured 0.93 (SD = 0.4), adaptive 1.41 (SD = 0.4); mixed ANOVA main effect of chatbot F(1, 358) = 60.93, p < 0.01; day F(1, 358) = 0.26, p = 0.61; chatbot x day F(1, 358) = 6.01, p = 0.02
contrasts.locator: p. 13, Section 7.2.1 Ideas similarity; Fig. 9 left (p. 14)

outcomes.name: Number of ideas generated by each group during idea generation
outcomes.question: none

contrasts.reported: Structured group generated 474 ideas, adaptive group 395; after filtering of too-similar ideas, 311 and 200 ideas went to review; no test reported

studies.label: Study 2: expert evaluation and non-randomized human-facilitated workshop baseline

assignment.what_was_assigned: A separate in-person workshop led by a human expert was compared with the existing chatbot groups from S1. No random allocation between the human workshop and chatbot conditions is reported; the expert was subsequently interviewed.
assignment.quote: We used them as a baseline to further analyze the chatbot-facilitated ideation.
assignment.locator: p. 17, Section 8 Expert evaluation; p. 19, Section 9 explicitly identifies Study 2

arms.name: Structured facilitator
arms.description: The structured chatbot group from S1 is reused for the comparison with the human workshop; this is not a newly randomized group in S2.

arms.name: Adaptive facilitator
arms.description: The adaptive chatbot group from S1 is reused for the comparison with the human workshop; this is not a newly randomized group in S2.

arms.name: Human facilitator (workshop baseline)
arms.description: An expert facilitated an hour-long in-person ideation workshop without chatbots, following the same ideation structure and goal. The stated workshop count conflicts with the demographic counts; no analysis-specific count is supplied.

participants.exclusions: No participant exclusions or analysis-specific counts are reported. The stated workshop total is internally inconsistent with its demographic counts, so the analyzed count is left null.
participants.who: The workshop is reported as having 11 participants (mean age 27.18, SD 7.55), but the same passage reports 8 men and 4 women, inconsistent with that total. Recruitment details and occupations of workshop participants are not stated. Separately, the interviewed facilitator was a woman aged 49 with over 25 years of facilitation experience; she is not counted as an ideating participant. The chatbot comparator samples are reused from S1, not additional participants.
participants.quote: The workshop was held for an hour with 11 participants (Mean age = 27.18, SD = 7.55, self-identified as men = 8 and women = 4)
participants.locator: p. 17, Section 8 Expert evaluation; p. 18, Fig. 11

ai_tool.name_model: No chatbot used in the human workshop; comparison groups reused the non-generative DistilBERT-based Telegram facilitators from S1
ai_tool.how_used: The expert independently led the workshop, then saw the chatbot demonstration and was interviewed. Neither the human workshop nor the reused chatbot conditions supplied generative-AI assistance (p. 17, Section 8; p. 9, Section 5.1).

task.description: Human-facilitated in-person idea generation and selection with the same pandemic-related goal and ideation structure as S1, followed by an expert interview; workshop ideas were compared non-randomly with S1 outputs (p. 17, Section 8).
task.duration: One hour for the workshop (p. 17, Section 8); interview duration not stated.

outcomes.name: Proportion of notable ideas retained after similarity filtering
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Notable ideas are those not filtered out as too similar or repetitive (p. 13, Fig. 7 caption; p. 26, Appendix A.3, similarity above 3.0 filtered out). Fig. 11 reports the group proportions. Comparisons use a chi-square test of independence with a Bonferroni correction (p. 17, Section 8). This is a retention proportion, not an expert creativity rating; the expert supplied an interview, not ratings of idea creativity.

contrasts.reported: Proportion of notable ideas: structured 0.66, human 0.64; structured versus human p > 0.1 (chi-square test of independence with Bonferroni correction). No chi-square statistic or confidence interval is printed.
contrasts.locator: p. 17, Section 8, first result bullet; p. 18, Fig. 11, top left

contrasts.reported: Proportion of notable ideas: adaptive 0.51, human 0.64; adaptive versus human p > 0.1 (chi-square test of independence with Bonferroni correction). No chi-square statistic or confidence interval is printed.
contrasts.locator: p. 17, Section 8, first result bullet; p. 18, Fig. 11, top left

outcomes.name: Semantic similarity of ideas to the fixed seed used in S1
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: The same fine-tuned DistilBERT seed-similarity measure used in S1 (p. 13, Section 7.2.1), with chatbot and human distributions compared by Kruskal-Walis H test and Dunn's post-hoc test (p. 17, Section 8; p. 18, Fig. 11, top right). Numerical means and standard deviations for the human baseline are not printed. Higher scores mean greater similarity to the seed, not a direct across-participant diversity measure.

contrasts.reported: Structured versus human idea similarity: p = 0.80 (Kruskal-Walis H test with Dunn's post-hoc test); no test statistic or human-baseline mean/SD is printed.
contrasts.locator: p. 17, Section 8, second result bullet; p. 18, Fig. 11, top right

contrasts.reported: Adaptive group idea similarity was higher than the human baseline: p < 0.01 (Kruskal-Walis H test with Dunn's post-hoc test); no test statistic or human-baseline mean/SD is printed.
contrasts.locator: p. 17, Section 8, second result bullet; p. 18, Fig. 11, top right

studies.label: Auxiliary human threshold calibration (Appendix A.3; not an ideation intervention)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Only the presentation order of prepared idea pairs was randomized for the raters. Pairs were also randomly sampled across classifier-score intervals. People were not assigned to generative-AI-assisted creation.
assignment.quote: 10 participants (Mean age = 24.80, SD = 4.26, 5 males) reviewed the selected pairs in a randomized order

arms.name: Human similarity raters
arms.description: Raters judged prepared idea pairs; there were no generative-AI assistance conditions.

participants.exclusions: Neutral-labeled pairs were excluded, and similar/very similar and dissimilar/very dissimilar labels were collapsed. The number of retained judgments and any post-exclusion rater count are not stated.
participants.who: 10 raters reviewed prepared pairs (mean age 24.80, SD 4.26, 5 males). Recruitment details are not stated. They supplied calibration judgments, not ideas created under assigned assistance; they are not added to S1.
participants.quote: 10 participants (Mean age = 24.80, SD = 4.26, 5 males) reviewed the selected pairs in a randomized order

ai_tool.how_used: Classifier predictions were calibrated against human labels of prepared pairs. This evaluated a scoring tool, not generative assistance to ideators (p. 26, Appendix A.3).

task.description: Rate similarity of 84 pairs sampled from 100 prepared ideas. Raters judged pairs in randomized order using a 5-point Likert scale (1 = very dissimilar; 5 = very similar); they did not generate creative output as an intervention task (p. 26, Appendix A.3, steps 1-4).

outcomes.name: Human similarity judgments used to calibrate classifier thresholds
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Neutral judgments were excluded; the retained number of ratings is not reported, so n_units is null. The paper reports classifier-human agreement of 83% at a similarity threshold of 2.0 and 84% at a very-similar threshold of 3.0 (p. 26, Appendix A.3, steps 4-6). These are calibration accuracies, not creativity effects or participant counts.

eligibility.reason: S1 randomized 48 people, 24 per arm, so it cannot have at least 50 people analyzed; its analysis-specific participant count remains unreported (pp. 11-12, Section 6.2 and Fig. 6). Both randomized arms used non-generative facilitation: retrieval of collaborators' ideas, predetermined prompts, fine-tuned DistilBERT similarity predictions and, for the adaptive condition, a bandit. GPT-4 was only benchmarked as a similarity classifier (pp. 7-10, Sections 4-5; p. 25, Appendix A). Criterion 3 is met for the output-level fluency measure: counts of generated ideas, a construct and category-count measure included in the codebook (p. 12, Section 7; p. 13, Fig. 7). Seed similarity is not a direct across-people diversity measure, and self-reported creativity support and satisfaction do not qualify (pp. 13-15, Sections 7.2-7.3). S2 adds a non-randomized human-workshop baseline with an internally inconsistent count, and S3 supplies human calibration judgments with randomized pair order; neither supplies randomized generative-AI assistance or additional S1 ideators (p. 17, Section 8; p. 26, Appendix A.3). Classifier benchmarks and bandit simulations also provide no eligible human creative-assistance study (pp. 25 and 28-29). No study meets all core criteria, and there is no eligible generative-AI context comparison.

one_line_finding: With 48 participants (24 per arm), ideas generated with the adaptive chatbot facilitator were more similar to a seed idea than those with the structured facilitator (mean 1.41 vs 0.93, F(1, 358) = 60.93, p < 0.01; p. 13), and the structured group produced more ideas (474 vs 395; p. 12).
open_questions: Section 8 (p. 17) reports an 11-participant workshop but also 8 men and 4 women. The internally inconsistent headcount cannot be resolved from this PDF; no corrected or analysis-specific count is supplied.
Appendix A.3 (p. 26) excludes neutral-labeled pairs without stating the retained number of ratings or any post-exclusion rater count; these counts remain null.
Appendix C (p. 27) refers to Supplementary.C but supplies no separate usable link. The local PDF includes Appendices A-D.
notes: Separate technical evaluations: Appendix A.1 (p. 25) compares fine-tuned DistilBERT and prompt-based GPT-4 (gpt-4-0613) predictions with human annotations on the SemEval2017-STS development and test sets. Appendix A.2 (p. 25) benchmarks response latency, testing each classifier 100 times on comparison/retrieval of an input sentence against 100 sentences; these are model runs and sentences, not people. GPT-4 was not deployed as assistance to ideators. The human threshold-calibration dataset is recorded separately as S3: 10 raters, 84 sampled pairs and 100 prepared ideas (p. 26, Appendix A.3). Only pair presentation order, not generative-AI assistance, was randomized for the raters; the retained rating count is unknown. Appendix D.1 (pp. 28-29, Fig. 12) evaluates the bandit in simulated idea-generation and idea-selection environments, including up to 50 trials; these trials do not represent randomized people. S2 reuses S1 chatbot outputs in its non-randomized comparisons; its human workshop and expert interview are separate from S1, and its participants cannot be added to S1 to meet the sample threshold (pp. 17-19, Sections 8-9). Expert interview findings and participant satisfaction, usability, creativity-support and self-rating measures are qualitative or self-reported evidence, not independent creativity ratings (pp. 12-18, Sections 6.4, 7.2.2, 7.3 and 8). S1 idea-similarity ANOVA degrees of freedom do not establish a participant analysis count; no participant-level standard error for this contrast is supplied (p. 13, Section 7.2.1; pp. 25-29, Appendices A-D). The full markdown, including references and Appendices A-D, was read; recorded numerical evidence was checked against the local PDF.
